input.title: Fix slice_start reporting success, then hanging, on an unsliceable plate
input.tldr: In the journey runs, every time the assistant switched to PETG and sliced, the slice tool said it had started but nothing was sliced, and a second try hung until the run timed out. This task finds out why and makes the tool report the real problem.
input.prompt:
Fix a bug in the JusPrin project assistant's `slice_start` tool. Repository: C:\src\JusPrin, branch jusprin-newui. Read AGENTS.md first (especially "Error handling discipline"), and write to the user (Kenneth) in plain English.

## The bug

When a plate cannot be sliced as configured, `slice_start` with `wait: true` returns success with no explanation, and a second call with `preempt: true, wait: true` never returns.

Seen repeatedly on 2026-10-13/14 in live "journey" runs of the in-app assistant (real app, real OrcaSlicer workspace, tool calls answered by the app). The setup each time: printer preset "Bambu Lab X1 Carbon 0.4 nozzle", plate type "Smooth Cool Plate" (the harness default), one small object (tests/data/jusprin/tee_with_hole.stl), filament switched by the assistant from "Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C" to "Bambu PETG HF @BBL X1C" with `printer_setup`. Then:

1. `slice_start {"wait": true}` returned state succeeded with
   `{"finished":false,"handle":"t-15","started":true,"slicing":{"jobs":[],"plates":[{"estimateStatus":"none","sliced":false,...}],"running":false}}`.
   So it claims the slice started, but nothing is running and nothing was sliced, and no reason is given.
2. `workspace_inspect {"sections":["slicing"]}` confirmed: not running, not sliced.
3. `slice_start {"preempt": true, "wait": true}` stayed in state `running` and never returned. The harness waited over 20 minutes before its deadline ended the run.

In a different run of the same setup, `slice_start` instead failed twice with the message "That plate cannot be sliced as it stands", and the assistant worked out that `cool_plate_temp` is 0 for PETG HF, switched the plate type to Engineering Plate, and then sliced successfully. So OrcaSlicer does know why the plate cannot be sliced (most likely the bed temperature for that plate type is 0 for this filament); the tool sometimes surfaces it and sometimes does not. When the person's plate was set to a textured PEI plate before slicing, the same PETG setup sliced fine.

## What to do

- Reproduce it. The tool is implemented in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp (search for SliceStart) with the slicing run in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp. The tool's contract is described in ToolRegistry.cpp under `slice_start`.
- Find why the first call reports `started: true` when OrcaSlicer refused or silently dropped the slice, and why the `wait` path of the second call never completes. Trace how upstream OrcaSlicer validates a plate before slicing (for example the bed-temperature / plate-type check and the notification it raises) and reuse its predicate rather than writing a copy.
- Fix it at the layer that owns the decision: a plate that cannot be sliced must come back as a failed call that says why in words the model can act on (which setting, which plate type), never as success, and a waiting call must always end. Do not paper over it with a timeout alone.
- Add tests: a unit or workspace-contract test for the refused-slice case, and if practical a shell harness check. tests/CLAUDE.md has the Catch2 rules.

## Evidence on disk (may be cleaned up later)

Journey records with the full call arguments and results:
C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--src-JusPrin\71e3bd46-c856-4b36-b7cc-979fe94e0bdf\scratchpad\exp\reversed\committed-prompt\outdoor-fitting-3.json and ...\reversed\multicall-all-loaded\outdoor-fitting-3.json (both ended with `"stopped": "deadline"`; look at the last turn's calls).

## Notes

- As of 2026-10-14 the journey harness (`shell_integration_harness --journey`, documented in tests/project_journey/README.md) is an UNCOMMITTED change in the main checkout C:\src\JusPrin, along with other uncommitted edits. Ask Kenneth whether it has been committed before relying on it; do not discard those changes. The bug can also be reproduced without it, through the MCP tools or a workspace-contract test.
- Any live model run needs Kenneth's approval of the run count and token estimate first. Reproducing this bug should not need a live model.
- Build notes for this Windows machine are in the memory file windows-build-machine.md.

**With deferral reversed, the assistant did what you expected, even on the prompt as committed.** In the "what is this part" conversation it read the object's geometry and asked for a picture of it. It then said what it thought the part was, a small T-shaped fitting with a 10 mm hole through it, and asked me to confirm. Once I said it was a garden-hose fitting that has to hold pressure, it recorded that and looked up the PETG filaments and process settings the printer actually has. It recommended PETG with a strength setting and explained how to orient the part around the hole. It also asked whether PETG was really loaded, instead of trusting the selected preset.

That is the behaviour you described at the start as hard to get. It came from the old prompt, with nothing changed except that the assistant could see its tools.

**What I still cannot show.** It asked for the picture but could not look at it, because the test model cannot view images. So "uses what it sees in the render" is still unproven.

**A real bug in the app, found on the way.** Every time the assistant switched to PETG and went to slice, the slice tool said it had started when nothing was actually sliced, and gave no reason. When the assistant tried again, the tool never came back and the run sat until it timed out. The cause is very likely that this PETG cannot be printed on the plate type the test starts with. I've put up a second task chip for it: "Fix slice_start reporting success, then hanging, on an unsliceable plate".

I'll give you the full comparison when the reruns finish.

content.text:
Yes, the conclusion holds. With the deferral commit actually reversed, the assistant does the job you described, even on the prompt you had before I changed anything.

**What I tested.** I rebuilt the app from the code as it was before tool deferral and ran the four conversations three times each on two prompts: the one you had committed, and my rewrite. A third set ran today's code with the multi-call fix and every tool visible. Twenty-one runs were interrupted by the model provider (rate limits, one host refusing requests); I set those aside and reran them, since they say nothing about the assistant.

**What happened.**

- **No conversation ended because of a refused tool call.** With deferral on, that is how every preparation ended.
- **Your old prompt was enough for the behaviour you wanted.** Asked what the part is, the assistant examined its shape first, guessed a T-shaped fitting with a 10 mm hole, and asked for confirmation. Told it holds hose pressure, it recorded that and looked up the PETG and process settings this printer actually has. It recommended PETG with a stronger setting and explained how to orient the part around the hole.
- **The preparation finished four times out of nine.** In those runs it recorded the purpose, switched to PETG, set the build plate, strengthened the walls and infill, sliced, and read the slice report.
- **The other five were stopped by the slicing bug, not by the assistant.** The slice tool says it started when nothing was sliced, then hangs on the retry. In four runs it stopped the conversation outright; one ran into the request limit while retrying the failed setup. That is the second task chip.

**Where the prompt rewrite still helps.** On "I want to print this", the old prompt once went straight to slicing the PLA setup without asking what the part was for. The rewrite never did. That kind of judgement is what the prompt is for; finding and calling tools is not.

**The multi-call fix, live.** The old app silently dropped 21 of the 144 tool calls the model made. The new one carried out all 123 of 123.

**Still unproven.** Whether the assistant uses what it sees in the rendered picture. It asks for the picture at the right moments, but this test model cannot see images. A model that can, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, would answer that; say if you want it run.

**Cost and state.** This round cost about 80 cents, bringing today's total to roughly $2.60 of the $8. Nothing is committed: the multi-call fix with its tests, the refusal message, the prompt rewrite, and the test harness are all in the working tree. Both task chips need the harness, so I'd suggest committing before starting them. Want me to commit?
Can you make the tool deferral revert into a separate commit?   And commit to whatever other things that you changed yourself into a clear commit with clear message about what they are about.

Root cause (diagnosed 2026-09-25, Entire CLI 0.11.0): when the committing session has file changes to link,
`entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` shows "Link this commit to session context? [Y/n]" and reads the
answer from `CONIN$`, not stdin. The agent's Git Bash has a hidden console, so the open succeeds and the read blocks forever.
`</dev/null` does not help. Commits with nothing to link skip the prompt, which is why it looked intermittent.
The log is buffered, so `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows nothing until the process exits.
Evidence: handle dump of the hung process showed a `\Device\ConDrv` handle with a blocked synchronous read.
Entire's own Pi integration prefixes agent bash commands with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` for this exact reason.
With `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` the same hook finished in ~0.3s and added the trailer, 3 of 3 runs; without it, 3 of 3 hung.

**Why:** It looks like a slow checkpoint condense, so it is easy to wait a long time for nothing.
A separate, real slowdown also exists: an `msbuild -m` build pins all 16 cores (processor queue ~64) and every
`entire` launch then takes 5-20s. That is slow, not hung; don't confuse the two.

**How to apply:** Fixed 2026-09-25: `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set as a user env var (HKCU\Environment), so Claude and Codex
shells inherit it after the app restarts (verified in Claude: 3/3 hook runs 0.3s with trailer). If a commit hangs again, first check
`echo $GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT` in the agent shell. Restarting the Claude app: the tray has no Quit, so end all `claude` processes
from a helper launched via WMI (outside Claude's tree) and relaunch with `explorer.exe shell:AppsFolder\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc!Claude`.
If one hangs anyway, kill only that commit's `entire` PID; never `--no-verify`. See [[windows-build-machine]].

2026-09-27: with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` already set, a `git merge --no-ff` (merge commit) in a worktree still ran past a
120 s `timeout` -- but the merge commit was already written correctly and nothing was left running. After a timeout, check
`git log -1` and the parents before retrying; a retry would make a second commit. A plain `git commit` minutes earlier took ~seconds.

Revert "Defer the project assistant's tools by default with hosted tool search"

This reverts commit 491b56d26b. Every tool is sent to the model loaded again,
as it was before.

With most tools hidden behind tool search, the assistant could not prepare a
print. The instructions name tools such as intent_update, presets_list,
object_analyze and plan_set. The model called them by name without searching
for them first, so it never saw their parameters, guessed the arguments, and
was refused. The third refusal in a turn ends the turn. In live runs of
scripted conversations (DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, every tool after
the first three deferred), 20 of 25 refused calls were such guesses, and no
attempt to prepare an outdoor PETG part ever reached a slice.

With this commit reverted and nothing else changed, the same conversations on
the same prompt had no turn ended by refused calls in 36 runs. The assistant
read the part's shape before guessing what it was, found PETG in the printer's
own preset list, and in 4 of 9 runs finished the preparation through slicing
and reading the slice report. The other runs were stopped by a separate
slice_start bug. The runs and how to repeat them are in
tests/project_journey/README.md, added in a following commit.

Deferral was only measured on OpenRouter with single-function deferral; the
built-in OpenAI route with namespaces was not tested. How to bring deferral
back without hiding the tools the instructions rely on is being investigated
separately.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

input.content:
Carry out every tool call the model makes in one reply

The project assistant asked the model for one tool call per reply
(parallel_tool_calls: false) and acted only on the first call it got. OpenAI
honours that request; DeepSeek through OpenRouter does not. In live runs the
model put several calls in one reply about one time in six, and the app
silently dropped the rest: 21 of 144 calls were never carried out and never
answered.

Now every call in a reply is carried out, one at a time, in the order the
model made them, and one request takes all the answers back. If a call fails
or is refused, the later calls of that reply that would change the project are
not carried out: the model made them before it could see the failure, so each
is answered "not run" and the model decides again. Read-only calls still run.
A picture returned by a call follows all the answers.

The request no longer asks for one call per reply. The limit dates from the
first version of the adapter; the one documented reason found, that OpenAI's
strict schemas did not hold for parallel calls, is no longer in OpenAI's
function-calling guide except for fine-tuned models. In live runs with this
change, 123 of 123 calls were carried out, 17 replies holding several.

tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py still asks for one call per reply
and acts on the first, so it no longer matches the app exactly when a model
makes several calls at once.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Record only what the person said, and look at the part before guessing what it is

The print guidance began "For a print request, record the user's explicit
purpose", which asked for a record even when no purpose had been given. Told
only "I want to print this on my X1 Carbon", the assistant recorded a purpose
nobody had stated ("General purpose tee fitting with hole") and PLA as the
material, both as confirmed by the user, in 2 of 3 runs.

The "Intent and setup" paragraph is now three:

- Intent: record a purpose or requirement when the person states one, in any
  turn, in their words. A file name, a selected preset or material and the
  assistant's own conclusions are not something the person said. When nothing
  has been stated, there is nothing to record.
- The object: when it matters what an object is and the person has not said,
  read its shape with object_analyze before judging, and offer the guess for
  the person to confirm.
- Setup: unchanged, except that it names presets_list as the way to find the
  filament and process presets this printer can use.

The intent_update description now says how the tool works, including its
assumed and question fields, which it never mentioned.

What this changed in live runs, with most tools then deferred: an invented
purpose on the first turn went from 2 of 3 runs to 0 of 3; reading the shape
before guessing went from 0 of 3 to 3 of 3; looking for a filament with
settings_search instead of presets_list went from 16 refused calls to 2. With
every tool loaded the assistant read the shape on its own with the old text
too, so "The object" mattered mostly while tools were hidden. What still
separates the two texts with every tool loaded: on "I want to print this" the
old text once sliced the PLA setup without asking what the part was for, and
this one never did.

Two side effects were seen and not resolved: the shape was read once or twice
when the person had already said what the part is, and a question was once
recorded as a requirement ("Considering PETG instead of PLA"). Runs and
numbers: tests/project_journey/README.md.

Add project assistant journeys: scripted conversations run in the real app

shell_integration_harness --journey <scenario.json> <output.json> opens a
model file the way a person adds one, so the assistant speaks first, then says
each scripted line to the live assistant. Every tool call is answered by the
app itself on a real project, so a long conversation stays about the project.
Earlier prompt tests answered calls with canned replies, which sent the model
wandering and cost about 200 million tokens.

The run records every reply, every call with its arguments and result, the
calls the adapter refused, each request's token usage, and the project as it
ended (presets, changed settings, intent, plan, slicing). It judges nothing:
each scenario lists questions for a person reading the record.

- The model is DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter on the hosts the printer
  prompt tests pin; the harness adds that routing, which the app does not send.
- --journey-experiment <file> replaces instruction text or tool descriptions
  in each request, so a wording can be tried without a build. The record keeps
  what was sent, and an edit that does not apply stops the run before any
  request.
- The model reads text only, so a picture returned by view_render is withheld
  and the model told so, instead of the request failing.
- A run that times out still saves what happened.
- LiveTransportLog and live_response_items come back from 491b56d26b, which
  was reverted: they log what each response held, which is how a call made
  without the tool in view was told apart from one made with it.

tests/project_journey/ has four scenarios, two that should change the project
and two that should only answer, and a README with how to run them and what
the runs so far found. Any live run needs Kenneth's approval of the run count
and token estimate first.

**Anthropic: reducing hallucinations**

Anthropic's official "Reduce hallucinations" guide lists three basic strategies. The first is letting the model admit uncertainty. Its own wording is that Claude should be explicitly given permission to say it doesn't know, and the guide says this can drastically reduce false information. A sample system prompt tells Claude to say "I don't know" or "I'm not sure" when it lacks enough information for a confident answer.

The second is grounding in direct quotes. For long documents (over 20k tokens), the guide suggests having Claude pull out word-for-word quotes before doing the task, which anchors its responses in the actual text.

The third is verifying with citations. The guide suggests Claude cite a source for each claim, and that it find a supporting quote for each claim after drafting. If it can't find a quote, it must retract the claim. The guide also says these techniques reduce hallucinations without eliminating them, which a secondary source summarizes as the guide stating that they significantly reduce hallucinations, they do not eliminate them entirely.

**OpenAI: agent guardrails and deterministic checks**

The search returned OpenAI's Agents SDK reference pages, not a conceptual guide to deterministic checks. Those reference pages describe input guardrails that run either in parallel with the agent or before it starts. A guardrail returns a result, and if its tripwire is set, the agent's execution will immediately stop. Output guardrails work the same way on the final response. The reference pages don't say "deterministic," so that framing comes from third-party sources.

Those sources describe a guardrail as a check that may use deterministic rules, schema validation, classifiers, another Large Language Model (LLM), human approval, or a combination of these methods. They recommend deterministic rules for anything that can be stated exactly, such as permission scopes, numeric limits, file paths, or allowed API operations. One source also argues that an independent guardrail can block an action even when the model ignores or misinterprets those instructions. These are secondary sources, so verify the details against OpenAI's documentation before relying on them.

**How the two fit together**

The Anthropic guidance works mainly at the prompt level: permission to abstain, quote extraction, and citation checks. The OpenAI SDK provides the enforcement layer, where code outside the model decides whether to halt, which is the kind of check the third-party sources recommend for exact rules. Neither approach eliminates hallucinations, so they are usually layered.

---
title: Reduce hallucinations
url: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
description: Minimize hallucinations in Claude's outputs by allowing uncertainty, grounding responses in direct quotes, and verifying claims with citations.
---

Even the most advanced language models, like Claude, can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context. This phenomenon, known as "hallucination," can undermine the reliability of your AI-driven solutions. This guide will explore techniques to minimize hallucinations and ensure Claude's outputs are accurate and trustworthy.

## Basic hallucination minimization strategies

* **Allow Claude to say "I don't know":** Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This simple technique can drastically reduce false information.

<Accordion title="Example: Analyzing a merger & acquisition report">
  ```text User wrap
  As our M&A advisor, analyze this report on the potential acquisition of AcmeCo by ExampleCorp.

  <report>
  {{REPORT}}
  </report>

  Focus on financial projections, integration risks, and regulatory hurdles. If you're unsure about any aspect or if the report lacks necessary information, say "I don't have enough information to confidently assess this."
  ```
</Accordion>

* **Use direct quotes for factual grounding:** For tasks involving long documents (>20k tokens), ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes first before performing its task. This grounds its responses in the actual text, reducing hallucinations.

<Accordion title="Example: Auditing a data privacy policy">
  ```text User wrap
  As our Data Protection Officer, review this updated privacy policy for GDPR and CCPA compliance.
  <policy>
  {{POLICY}}
  </policy>

  1. Extract exact quotes from the policy that are most relevant to GDPR and CCPA compliance. If you can't find relevant quotes, state "No relevant quotes found."

  2. Use the quotes to analyze the compliance of these policy sections, referencing the quotes by number. Only base your analysis on the extracted quotes.
  ```
</Accordion>

* **Verify with citations**: Make Claude's response auditable by having it cite quotes and sources for each of its claims. You can also have Claude verify each claim by finding a supporting quote after it generates a response. If it can't find a quote, it must retract the claim.

<Accordion title="Example: Drafting a press release on a product launch">
  ```text User wrap
  Draft a press release for our new cybersecurity product, AcmeSecurity Pro, using only information from these product briefs and market reports.
  <documents>
  {{DOCUMENTS}}
  </documents>

  After drafting, review each claim in your press release. For each claim, find a direct quote from the documents that supports it. If you can't find a supporting quote for a claim, remove that claim from the press release and mark where it was removed with empty [] brackets.
  ```
</Accordion>

***

## Advanced techniques

* **Chain-of-thought verification**: Use [thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking) with `display: "summarized"`, and review the summarized reasoning in the `thinking` blocks when an answer looks wrong. This can reveal faulty logic or assumptions.

* **Best-of-N verification**: Run Claude through the same prompt multiple times and compare the outputs. Inconsistencies across outputs could indicate hallucinations.

* **Iterative refinement**: Use Claude's outputs as inputs for follow-up prompts, asking it to verify or expand on previous statements. This can catch and correct inconsistencies.

* **External knowledge restriction**: Explicitly instruct Claude to only use information from provided documents and not its general knowledge.

<Note>
  Remember, while these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions.
</Note>

content.text:
Partly, yes. One sentence in that commit is exactly the kind of patch you mean. The rest is either a product instruction, or the removal of a rule that was causing the error in the first place. The commit has three parts:

- **The rule that caused the invented purpose.** The old text said "for a print request, record the user's purpose", which demanded a record even when the person had given no purpose. The model obliged by inventing one. Removing that demand undoes a mistake the prompt itself made, so it is not a hallucination patch.
- **"Record their words, not your inferences… or mark them assumed."** This one is a patch, and you're right that it's hacky. It also only half worked: no run ever marked anything as assumed. The underlying problem is in the app, not the model. Today the app records every intent field as "confirmed by the user" unless the model volunteers otherwise. In other words, the app takes the model's word for where a fact came from. A different model will make that mistake in a different way, and no sentence will cover them all.
- **"Look at the part before guessing what it is."** This describes behaviour you want from the product, so it belongs in the instructions. Naming `presets_list` was only there to make up for hidden tools, and isn't needed now that every tool is visible.

## What the guidance online says

The sources agree closely:

- **Rules that must always hold are enforced in code, not in prompts.** The model's output is treated as untrusted. JusPrin already does this for tool arguments, since every call is checked against its schema and a call to an unknown tool is refused. It does not do it for where a value came from. One paper calls this "tool content hallucination": arguments filled in with things the user never said. The suggested fix is to check that a value can be traced to the conversation, and to block or downgrade it when it can't.
- **The model should have a way out other than guessing.** Anthropic's guide puts "let the model say it doesn't know" first. The same paper adds asking the user as an explicit option.
- **Ground claims in the source and verify them.** Anthropic suggests having the model quote the exact words its claim rests on. It also says plainly that these techniques reduce hallucination but don't eliminate it, so critical facts still need checking.
- **For an app that must work across models:**
  - keep the core instructions free of steering for one model;
  - treat abilities some models lack (pictures, tool search, several calls per reply) as declared capabilities that the app checks;
  - judge behaviour per provider, not as one blended score.

For the intent record, that points to a fix that works on any model. The tool would ask for the person's own words behind each confirmed field. The app would check those words actually appear in what the person said. Anything it can't trace would be stored, and shown, as the assistant's assumption.

One tension worth knowing about: our prompt evaluations run on DeepSeek only. That keeps cost and noise down, but wording tuned there may not carry over to other models. Guarantees enforced in code do carry over.

## The note in agent-docs

I added it to the "Governing decisions" list in [agent-docs/jusprin/README.md](agent-docs/jusprin/README.md). It says:

- JusPrin must work with whichever model a person configures, from any provider, even though few are wired up today.
- What must always hold is enforced by the app and its tools, not by instruction wording.
- The instructions describe what the product wants, not corrections for one model's errors.
- Abilities some models lack are checked by the app, which keeps working without them.

It's not committed yet.

## Decision for you

Should I rework that commit along these lines? I'd drop the patch sentence, keep the product instructions, and move the "only record what the person actually said" guarantee into `intent_update` itself, with tests.

Sources:
- [Anthropic: Reduce hallucinations](https://platform.claude.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [Reducing Tool Hallucination via Reliability Alignment (Relign)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.04141)
- [Phantom tool calls: when AI agents invoke tools that don't exist](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/04/14/phantom-tool-calls-when-ai-agents-invoke-tools-that-dont-exist)
- [agentvet: validating LLM tool arguments](https://docs.rs/crate/agentvet/0.1.0)
- [OpenAI Agents SDK: guardrails reference](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/guardrail/)
- [Cross-model and cross-provider policy portability (Gravitee)](https://gravitee.io/corpus/gen-982/hope-i/cross-model-and-cross-provider-policy-portability-for-ai-agent-and-llm-gateways.html)
- [AI agent portability: switching models without rebuilding (MintMCP)](https://www.mintmcp.com/blog/ai-agent-portability)

I'll add those now: automatic outcome checks in each scenario, a runner and a comparison script in the repo, a baseline from the runs that match the committed code, and a short "how to check your change" section in the README.

## Running one

Before any live run, Kenneth approves the number of runs and the token
estimate. Building the harness authorizes nothing.

```sh
shell_integration_harness --journey tests/project_journey/scenarios/outdoor-fitting.json /tmp/outdoor-fitting.json
```

It needs `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, which the printer prompt tests keep in
`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env`; never print it or put it in a command. The
harness and the Agent page must be built from the same commit.

`--journey-experiment <file>` changes what one run sends without a build:
`{"name": ..., "replace": [{"find": ..., "with": ...}], "instructions": ...,
"toolDescriptions": {"tool": ...}}`. Each `find` must occur exactly once in
the instructions or the run stops before its first request, and the record
keeps the instructions and tool descriptions that were sent.

One pass of the four scenarios took 363,228 input tokens (200,960 of them
cached) and 17,491 output tokens over 48 requests on 2026-10-13, with most
tools deferred. With every tool loaded and the fourth `outdoor-fitting` line,
a pass took 2.2 to 2.6 million input tokens, four fifths of them cached.
Report each batch's actual usage.

## A scenario

```json
{
  "name": "outdoor-fitting",
  "model": "tests/data/jusprin/tee_with_hole.stl",
  "turns": ["I want to print this.", "..."],
  "maxRequestsPerTurn": 20,
  "timeoutSeconds": 900,
  "review": ["Was the purpose recorded once it was stated?", "..."]
}
```

The project starts as the harness starts every project: a Bambu Lab X1 Carbon
with a 0.4 mm nozzle and the filament and process OrcaSlicer selects for it.
`model` is opened as a person opens a file, so the assistant speaks first and
that opening message is the record's first turn. A turn is said when the
previous reply has ended. `maxRequestsPerTurn` (default 20) ends the run when
one turn makes more requests than that, and the record says `request_cap`.

The lines are fixed, so a line cannot answer a question the script did not
expect. Write each line to stand on its own, and read a reply that asked
something else as a finding, not as a broken run.

## The record

- `turns`: for each turn, what was said, each reply, each call with its
  arguments, state, error and result (the first 6,000 characters of a larger
  one), whether the call changes the project, and each request's token usage.
- `refusedCalls`: calls the adapter refused before they ran (an unknown tool,
  arguments that miss the contract).
- `project`: the printer, filament and process selected at the end, every
  setting that differs from its preset, and `workspace_inspect`'s summary,
  objects, intent, plan, slicing and printer sections.
- `usage`: requests and tokens for the whole run.
- `stopped`: `completed`, `turn_failed` or `request_cap`.

## Reading a record

These carry over from the skills experiment's
[lessons](https://github.com/TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin/blob/feature/project-skills-routing/tests/project_prompt/README.md#preserved-lessons-from-the-original-branch).

- Judge the outcome: what the project ended as, what was recorded, and what
  the last reply claims. Which tool came first and how many questions were
  asked are the path, and a path check rewards the wording it was tuned on.
- A scenario that should act has a partner that should only answer
  (`outdoor-fitting` and `petg-question`, `desk-ornament` and `what-is-this`).
  A change that helps one must not break the other.
- One run is one sample. Do not rewrite the prompt for a single surprising
  record: read the trace first, and compare old and new text in the same batch
  before believing a difference.
- A number quoted from these runs names the scenario and the date, and is
  taken out when the scenario turns out to be flawed.

## First pass, 2026-10-13

const section = `## Checking a change for regressions

Do this for any change to what the assistant reads or calls: its instructions,
a tool's description or contract, or the Agent adapter.

1. Get two harness builds: one from the commit before your change and one with
   it. Copy \`shell_integration_harness\` aside under another name before you
   rebuild, or use a second build tree. A change to instruction wording or a
   tool description needs only one build: write the old text into an
   \`--experiment\` file (see "Running one") and run both from the same binary.
2. Get Kenneth's approval for the spend. One batch is the four scenarios three
   times, about 2.5 million input tokens, a quarter of a dollar at list price.
3. Run both batches close together, since the model's hosts vary by the hour:

   \`\`\`sh
   node tests/project_journey/run_journeys.mjs --harness <before build> --out <dir>/before
   node tests/project_journey/run_journeys.mjs --harness <after build> --out <dir>/after
   \`\`\`

   Two batches can run at the same time; more than that trips the provider's
   rate limits. A run the provider interrupts is set aside and run again.
4. Compare: \`node tests/project_journey/check.mjs <dir>/before <dir>/after\`.
   Each scenario's \`expect\` block lists outcome checks, and every run must
   also finish without a refused call. A check that passes in every run on one
   side and at most one on the other is marked \`<<\`.
5. Read the records the checker lists as failing, and read the replies against
   each scenario's \`review\` questions. A drop marked \`<<\` is a regression
   until the records show another cause. A smaller difference is noise at
   three runs: read the records instead of buying more runs.

The checks stand in for some questions only roughly. \`noPurposeBeforeTurn\`
treats any title recorded before the person said what the part is for as made
up. \`sliced\` also fails when \`slice_start\` misbehaves, which is not the
assistant's doing. Nothing checks how the assistant uses a picture, because the
model cannot see one.

### Baseline

BASELINE_PLACEHOLDER

`;

s = s.replace('  "timeoutSeconds": 900,\n  "review": ["Was the purpose recorded once it was stated?", "..."]',

fs.writeFileSync(f, s);
for (const k of ['BASELINE_PLACEHOLDER', '"expect": {"recordsPurposeInTurn"', '`deadline` when', 'holds the outcome checks']) if (!s.includes(k)) console.log('MISSING ' + k);

content.text:
Future agents now have a working way to check their change. It's tested end to end on the committed code, but not committed yet.

**What an agent does:**

1. Build the test harness twice, once before its change and once after. If the change is only to instruction wording or a tool description, one build is enough, with the old text passed in a small file.
2. Get your approval for the spend. One batch is about 25 cents.
3. Run both batches with the new runner, `run_journeys.mjs`. It runs the four conversations three times each, keeps one record per run, reruns any run the model provider broke, and stops at a spending cap or if the key is refused.
4. Compare the two batches with the new checker, `check.mjs`. Each scenario now lists the outcomes it should reach, such as "ended on PETG", "project left unchanged" or "purpose recorded". The checker counts how many runs reached each one on each side, and marks a check that held every time before and at most once after.
5. Read the records the checker lists as failing, and the replies against each scenario's review questions. The scripts can only check what is mechanical; whether the advice is good still needs reading.

AGENTS.md now has one line telling agents to do this for any change to what the assistant reads or calls.

**Proving it works.** As a test of the runner, I recorded a baseline on the committed code, for about 17 cents. Everything passed except two things:

- Two of the three fitting runs hung on the known slicing bug.
- Two "what is this" runs each had one call refused that the assistant then corrected.

Comparing that baseline against the old deferral-era runs, the checker correctly flagged the three big differences the revert made.

**Two of my checks were wrong, and I fixed them.** One counted any title recorded early as an invented purpose. But "Print a tee with a hole" is just a description, and a script can't tell the two apart, so that stays a question for a person reading the record. The other check credited a slice that happened earlier in the conversation; it now looks only at how the project ended.

**Not committed yet:** the runner, the checker, the scenario checks, the README section with the baseline, the AGENTS.md line, and last turn's agent-docs note about supporting every model. Should I commit them? I'd make two commits: the agent-docs note on its own, and the regression kit with the AGENTS.md pointer.

content.text:
I've pulled `jusprin-newui`: it fast-forwarded cleanly to `336facf825`, and the main checkout is clean.

## What we did in this session

**The question.** You asked why the assistant struggles with basic things, like choosing a suitable filament preset, or looking at a model and guessing what it is. You'd tried adding more rules to the prompt (commit `55a2d37618`), which helped little and broke other cases.

**How I investigated.**
- I read the abandoned skills branch to learn from its testing mistakes.
- I built a test harness that runs scripted conversations in the real app, with the app answering every tool call, and wrote four conversations to run in it.
- I ran about 400 of those conversations across a series of experiments, for roughly $3 of the $8 you allowed.

**What we found.**
- The prompt was not too complicated, and the model was not short of knowledge. Cut to six sentences, it still knew PLA is wrong for a part left in the sun and that PETG suits it.
- The real cause was tool deferral (`491b56d26b`). It hid most tools from the model, while the prompt told the model to use them by name. The model called them without being able to see their parameters, guessed the arguments, and was refused. Three refusals end a turn, so no preparation ever finished.
- With every tool visible, your old prompt did the job. The assistant examined the part's shape, guessed it was a T-fitting with a hole and asked you to confirm, found PETG in the printer's own preset list, and in several runs finished the preparation through slicing.

**Problems found along the way.**
- The app silently dropped any extra tool calls when the model made several at once.
- The slice tool reports a slice as started when nothing was sliced, then hangs on the retry. This stopped most PETG preparations.
- Whether the assistant makes good use of the rendered picture can't be tested on DeepSeek V4 Flash, because it can't see images.

**The principle we settled on.** From your pushback and the guidance online: rules that must always hold go in code, not prompt wording, because different models make different mistakes.

**What became of the code.** The deferral revert, the multi-call fix, the prompt rewrite, the harness, and the regression runner and checker are all on branch `claude/project-assistant-journeys` and were not adopted. Two task sessions were started from it: one on deferral, one on the slicing bug.

## How the new commits affect that

- **Deferral is gone from the branch history.** It was removed in the rewrite rather than by a revert, so my revert commit is now pointless. The deferral-fix session built on `491b56d26b`, which is no longer in the history. If deferral comes back, it should be rebuilt fresh, with one rule from what we found: every tool the prompt names must be visible to the model.
- **The prompt now lives on the Agent page, in `projectInstructions.ts`, unchanged and pinned by a test.** That's a good place to evaluate edits from. My harness's experiment option still applies, because it edits the text in the outgoing request wherever the text comes from. But my branch would no longer merge cleanly: the harness file has changed in several places since.
- **"Ask AI" now gets every tool.** Before, the app itself prevented a "just explain" turn from changing the project. Now only the prompt sentence "a question… is not by itself a request to change the project" stands guard. That is the prompt-only kind of rule we just agreed is fragile across models, so it's worth a deliberate decision.
- **No more save-or-discard refusals.** `project_open` and `printer_setup` no longer refuse over unsaved work, which removes two ways a preparation could get stuck on a refused call. The flip side is that `printer_setup` now drops unsaved preset edits and lists them. If the assistant tunes settings before switching filament, that tuning could be lost. In our runs it usually switched first, but this should be rechecked.
- **Still open:**
  - The app still asks for one tool call per reply and drops the extras, since the multi-call fix wasn't adopted.
  - The slicing bug has no fix on the branch yet.
  - None of the journeys has been run against the new branch, so nothing has measured what these commits change in practice.

time; after each result the adapter hands it the next, and once the last
has its result, all the results go back to the model in one request,
each under its own call id, with any images after them. When a call does
not succeed (failed, cancelled, or refused for unknown tools or bad
arguments), the calls after it in that response are not run: each gets a
"not_run" result naming the call that failed, so the model sees why and
can decide again. This follows OpenAI's and Anthropic's guidance to
return a result for every call.

Tests: the request flag; two calls run in order with both results in one
request; a failed or cancelled call and a refused call each leave the
later calls unrun; images follow all the results. Five of these fail on
the previous adapter. All 293 agent test cases and the default shell
harness pass. An end-to-end run of the real app (the prompt recorder
with a throwaway script) ran workspace_inspect and intent_update from one
response, and answered an intent_update unrun after a settings_apply_patch
failed with stale_workspace.


=================== c7ed56d027
Record why a slice did not succeed, make slicing asynchronous, and add the slice-failed skill

When OrcaSlicer refused a plate, slice_start answered "started", and with
wait it hung for 15 minutes with no reason. Each plate now carries why its
last slice did not succeed (refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the
setting and object), recorded through a hook in Plater::reslice and the
run's completion event, in the print-issue monitor's words. It shows in the
workspace block, tool replies and slice_report. slice_start decides inside
the call whether a run began, the plates were already sliced, or OrcaSlicer
refused. There is no wait: a run goes on in the background, its card sits
below the call, and the reply states those facts. When the model's run ends
after its turn, the app posts a note and starts a turn on it. The
slice-failed skill fires on the first request that carries a new failure.
The standing prompt now says to assume a beginner. The eval gains two
refusal cases, the recorder can press Slice and Slice all, and
requests.json is re-recorded. The shell harness waits for the page's active
chat before scripted sends.


=================== 3341abf38f
Record the reads Opus 5.5 sends, and tell intent_update to record only a stated purpose

Squash of claude/opus-recorded-reads (24303e3a67, e7b7db2c69), re-recorded
on jusprin-newui after the file-load facts and skill rewrite.

Recorded reads. The first --backend claude-cli batch (2026-10-19) left 10 of
63 runs unobserved, nearly all because Opus 5.5 asked for one of two reads
DeepSeek V4 Flash never sent, so the recording held no answer:
- a changedOnly settings_search of each object (scope "object", empty query);
- slice_report of a plate other than the active one.
script.json's answers list now records slice_report for every plate by
plateId and the changedOnly search for every object on every plate.
recorded_answer in run_prompt_tests.py answers a changedOnly search from a
recorded one with the same scope, target and query, whatever its limit, and
never mixes searches with and without changedOnly. test_steps.py gains a test
for each read; the changedOnly one fails with the old rule.

intent_update. In print-this-no-purpose ("I want to print this", nothing said
about what it is for), Opus 5.5 called intent_update in 6 of 6 runs with a
guessed purpose marked assumed. Kenneth decided the model should ask first,
so the description now says never to record a purpose the person has not
stated, even marked assumed. The schema and the case are unchanged; this is
the only change outside tests (ToolRegistry.cpp, one description).

project_tools.json is regenerated with JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1
agent_bridge_tests '[project]'. requests.json is re-recorded with the shell
harness and the Agent page bundle built from this tree, so its file-load
points carry the new report facts and the rewritten file-loaded skill.

Subscription runs on the branch before the re-record (claude-cli backend and
judge, 3 each): print-this-no-purpose 1 passed, 2 failed (each asked two
questions where the case allows one; none recorded a guessed purpose);
prepare-petg-strong 3 passed; after-intent 3 passed.


=================== 57b58cb268
Merge intent_update and plan_set into one tool, setup_record

The setup card's title (what the person wants) and its headline (how the
agent will print it) were written by two tools, and the model kept them apart
badly: in batch B's changed-strategy journeys (2026-10-19) it rewrote the
headline with plan_set but never called intent_update, so the card read
"dried flowers, spiral vase" above "watertight multi-wall". The two records
were already handled as one (same coordinator block, both in-app only, both
on the chat, the same context push), so they are now one tool.

setup_record takes, all at the top level:
- purpose, required on every call, at most 60 characters: what the person
  wants the print to be or do, in a few words and their terms, not how to
  print it (no settings, material, printer or print mode unless the person
  made one of them the goal). It titles the setup card.
- fields, optional, with intent_update's semantics (assumed, question,
  provenance).
- headline, decisions, unverified, risks: the plan, optional. With a
  headline they replace the whole plan; with none the plan is kept, so a
  purpose can be recorded before there is a strategy. unverified is one
  sentence per thing taken as true without being able to check.
The result carries the intent section, purposeChange and the setup in force,
and always the plan as it now stands. The card's context is pushed once per
successful call, so title and headline arrive together.

The setup-changed skill fires on a first purpose or changed fields, as
before; a new purpose wording alone is title_only, and a call that only
restates the purpose to change the plan is unchanged, so neither fires it.

Why it looks like this (DeepSeek V4 Flash, live runs of 2026-10-19/20):
- "purpose", not "setupTitle": under either tool 7 of 12 batch-B titles,
  and some batch-C titles, described the setup ("Rhino figurine — 0.16mm,
  3 walls, organic supports"); with the rename and the description every
  title in two later batches was goal-only.
- A flat plan, not a nested object: the model sent the nested plan as a
  string of JSON, which the registry refuses; two refusals end a turn.
- "unverified", not "assumptions": next to fields' "assumed" flag, the
  model put intent-field objects under assumptions. This last rename has
  not been run live.

=================== 8a3db9052d
Remove the PETG-on-Cool-Plate prompt case

petg-on-cool-plate expected the assistant, told "ok, print it" after a
switch to Bambu PETG HF, to notice on its own that the Smooth Cool Plate
cannot print that filament. That is an OrcaSlicer slice-time rule the setup
preview does not report, so the case measured what the model knows about
Bambu presets rather than whether it follows the prompt. It also failed
slicing, the step the prompt asks for before a print is called ready. A
problem like this belongs in the tools' results; a case can come back once
slicing reports OrcaSlicer's reason.

The case, its conversation in script.json and its recording are gone; the
other 24 recordings are unchanged, and no setting item was left unused. The
run budget goes to 72, three runs for each of the 24 cases. The recorder's
plateType option and its wait before each new message stay:
print-this-no-purpose uses the first, and the second keeps any message after
a setup change honest.


=================== 87b3c50474
Name each plate's type in the project chat's workspace block

The <workspace> block sent with every project chat turn listed each plate's
id, name, active and sliced state and its objects, but not its plate type.
In live chats the assistant switched a project on a Smooth Cool Plate to
Bambu PETG HF, which OrcaSlicer will not slice on that plate, and only found
out when the slice stalled.

Each plate now carries plateType, the name printer_setup and its preview
use, with OrcaSlicer's untranslated plate names (the values plate_layout's
bedType takes). The workspace snapshot reads it from the plate the way
plate_layout writes it: the plate's own choice, else the project's. A plate
with no type gets no field rather than a null, and an unchanged project
sends the same bytes on every turn.

Tests: the request body check and a new test for the field, its absence and
byte stability; a fake-workspace contract test and a real-adapter harness
check that a plate_layout choice is what the snapshot reports. The project
prompt requests are recorded again; only the new field, timestamps and a
temporary path changed. The prompt text is unchanged.

The harness config now points OrcaSlicer's startup version check at a
closed local port. The check runs even in stealth mode, and since
v2.5.0-alpha was published on 2026-10-16 it opened a modal "new version"
dialog that stopped every shell harness run, the re-recording included.

content.text:
Mostly yes. The four concrete problems we found are each addressed by a commit since the last pull, and two smaller gaps remain. I read this from the remote branch only, because the main checkout has another session's uncommitted edits in it.

**Fixed:**

- **Dropped tool calls.** `64350306c9` now runs every call in a reply, in order. If one fails, the rest are answered "not run" so the model can decide again. That is the same design as my unadopted fix. It survives the later move to one turn loop shared by OpenAI, OpenRouter and Anthropic.
- **The slicing bug.** `c7ed56d027`: when OrcaSlicer refuses a plate, the slice tool now says so inside the call, with OrcaSlicer's reason and the setting and object involved. The tool no longer waits, so nothing hangs: slicing runs in the background, and when it ends the app posts a note and starts a turn on it. There is also a new skill for when a slice fails.
- **PETG on the Cool Plate.** `87b3c50474` tells the model each plate's type on every turn. That, together with the slicing fix, gives it what it needs to catch the mismatch.
- **Invented purposes.** This is handled two ways:
  - `57b58cb268` merges `intent_update` and `plan_set` into one tool, `setup_record`, whose `purpose` field must describe the goal, not the settings.
  - `3341abf38f` changes the tool's description to say never to record a purpose the person hasn't stated, even marked as assumed.

  The second part is still a wording rule, not a check in code. That is the kind of model-specific patch we discussed, though it now lives in the tool's description, not the prompt.
- **Looking at the model.** The new "file loaded" skill (`4ec21799ce`) has the app attach a picture of the plate to the first request after a file opens. So the assistant looks at the object without having to decide to call `view_render`.
- **Other models.** `170d1ae080` adds Anthropic and OpenRouter as providers, and models can now be chosen per chat.
- **Tool deferral.** It is still absent from the code, so the blind-call failure can't recur.

**Still open:**

- **Pictures sent to a model that can't see them.** The app now always sends a plate picture after a file opens. In our runs, OpenRouter refused any request with a picture for DeepSeek V4 Flash, and the turn failed. The new prompt test runner works around this by not replaying pictures, but I found no check in the app itself. Someone using DeepSeek V4 Flash in the app may get a failed first message. I haven't confirmed this with a live run.
- **"Ask AI" turns can change the project.** The new sectioned prompt treats "Explain this issue and my options" as a question, but nothing in code stops such a turn from changing the project.
- **Whole preparations aren't measured.** The new prompt test suite judges one step at a time from recorded points in a real chat, and a change ends the run. So nothing measures a preparation from first message through slicing. My journey harness did that, but it was not adopted.
